Cannabis 101

Cannabis Rescheduling Explained for Michigan Shoppers

Federal rescheduling has moved in stages since 2022. Here is what has changed as of October 2026, what has not, and what it means at a Michigan counter.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 202610 min read

10min readCannabis 101
In this article
  1. The Controlled Substances Act schedules in brief
  2. Rescheduling vs. descheduling
  3. How cannabis rescheduling got here: a dated timeline
  4. What the April 2026 order does now
  5. What Schedule III could change: research and the 280E cannabis tax
  6. What rescheduling doesn't change
  7. At the counter in Michigan: what changes for shoppers
  8. Next steps to watch
  9. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • As of October 2026, only marijuana drugs approved by the FDA and marijuana covered by a state medical marijuana license are in Schedule III; adult-use marijuana is still Schedule I.
  • A broader proposal to move all marijuana to Schedule III went to a DEA hearing in summer 2026, and the judge's recommended decision was still pending in late October.
  • The April 2026 order says state medical licensees are no longer subject to the Section 280E deduction ban, and it eases some research access.
  • Nothing changes at a Michigan counter for adult-use shoppers: 21 and older, valid ID at every sale, same purchase limits.
  • Federal law still forbids carrying cannabis over a state line, even when both states allow it.

Did cannabis get rescheduled? Partly: cannabis rescheduling has moved in stages since 2022. As of October 2026, only two groups of marijuana products sit in Schedule III: drugs approved by the FDA and marijuana covered by a state medical marijuana license. Everything else, including adult-use cannabis, is still Schedule I under federal law.

Here is what the schedules mean, how we got here and what it all means at a Michigan counter.

The Controlled Substances Act schedules in brief

The Controlled Substances Act, passed in 1970, sorts regulated drugs into five schedules. Placement depends on a drug's potential for abuse, whether it has a currently accepted medical use and how much dependence it can cause. When Congress passed the law, it put marijuana in Schedule I.

ScheduleWhat the law saysExamples from federal documents
IHigh potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use, a lack of accepted safety under medical supervisionHeroin, LSD, ecstasy, and adult-use marijuana
IIHigh potential for abuse, an accepted medical use, and abuse may lead to severe dependenceCocaine, methamphetamine, oxycodone, fentanyl
IIILower abuse potential than I and II, an accepted medical use, and moderate or low physical dependenceKetamine, anabolic steroids, some codeine products, and since April 2026, state-licensed medical marijuana
IV and VLower abuse potential and more limited dependence than the schedule above each oneNot part of the marijuana proposals

A drug's schedule sets how tightly it's controlled: who may make or handle it, what records they keep and how research works. A schedule doesn't, by itself, make a drug legal to buy.

The law gives the Attorney General the power to schedule, reschedule or remove a drug, and that power is delegated to the head of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The federal health department, HHS, supplies a scientific and medical evaluation. A review can start at the Attorney General's own initiative, at HHS's request or through a petition from any interested party.

Petitions to reschedule marijuana are nothing new. The DEA turned them down in 2001, 2011 and twice in 2016, and in 2016 HHS agreed that marijuana still met the criteria for Schedule I. In its 2023 review, HHS reached a different view: that marijuana has a lower potential for abuse than drugs in Schedules I and II. For what research says about cannabis's risks, see our look at common cannabis myths.

Rescheduling vs. descheduling

Rescheduling moves a drug from one schedule to another. It remains a controlled substance with federal rules attached. The 2024 proposal was explicit on this point: even in Schedule III, making, distributing, dispensing and possessing marijuana would stay subject to the federal law's criminal provisions.

Descheduling removes a substance from the Controlled Substances Act altogether. Hemp is the familiar example. It's excluded from the federal definition of marijuana, and the April 2026 order says it doesn't change hemp's status. Our guide to hemp vs. marijuana explains where that line falls.

So the rescheduling vs. descheduling question comes down to this: one changes the level of federal control, and the other ends it.

How cannabis rescheduling got here: a dated timeline

Marijuana rescheduling has unfolded over four years, and the dates matter:

DateWhat happened
Oct. 6, 2022President Biden asked the Attorney General and the HHS Secretary to review how marijuana is scheduled.
Aug. 29, 2023HHS recommended moving marijuana to Schedule III.
May 21, 2024The Justice Department proposed moving marijuana to Schedule III.
Aug. 29, 2024The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced a hearing on the proposal.
Jan. 13, 2025The judge overseeing the hearing stayed the proceedings pending an appeal filed by two participants. The stay never lifted, and the hearing never took place.
December 2025Executive Order 14370 directed the Attorney General to complete the rescheduling process as quickly as federal law allows.
Apr. 28, 2026A final federal order moved marijuana drugs approved by the FDA, and marijuana covered by a state medical marijuana license, to Schedule III, effective that day. The DEA also withdrew the 2024 hearing notice and scheduled a new hearing.
June 29 to July 15, 2026The DEA's chief administrative law judge heard 11 days of testimony on the broader proposal.
Late October 2026The judge allowed extra written briefs, with replies due Nov. 5, and kept the case on hold until briefing closed. His recommended decision was still pending, and no final decision on moving all marijuana had been published.

That leaves two tracks. A narrower order covering medical marijuana and drugs approved by the FDA is already in effect. The broader proposal, which covers all marijuana including adult-use, is still working its way through.

Why did the medical track move first? The April order relied on a separate part of the law tied to U.S. treaty obligations under the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs. That route lets the Attorney General place a drug by order, without the findings and rulemaking steps, including a hearing, that the usual path requires. The broader proposal follows the standard path, which is why it went back to a hearing.

What the April 2026 order does now

For now, Schedule III marijuana means two things: drug products approved by the FDA that contain marijuana, and marijuana in any form covered by a state medical marijuana license. Any other marijuana remains a Schedule I substance, with the same federal controls as before.

For state medical licensees, the order created an expedited path to register with the DEA. Applications filed within 60 days of publication are to be processed within six months, and early applicants may keep operating under their state licenses while they wait. A federal registration is automatically suspended if the state license is suspended, revoked or expires, so federal approval tracks the state's. These registrations don't authorize non-medical use.

The order also adds permit requirements for importing and exporting these products. Prescriptions are required before marijuana drug products approved by the FDA are dispensed, except when a DEA-registered practitioner dispenses them directly.

What Schedule III could change: research and the 280E cannabis tax

Section 280E

Section 280E of the federal tax code bars businesses that traffic in Schedule I or II substances from deducting ordinary business expenses. That has kept cannabis businesses from taking deductions most other businesses take for granted.

The April 2026 order says state medical marijuana licensees will no longer be subject to 280E, because the provision applies only to Schedules I and II. It adds that it isn't a determination of anyone's tax liability and that licensees should consult tax counsel. The order's 280E note covers state medical licensees; adult-use marijuana remains in Schedule I. The 2024 proposal noted that if all marijuana moves to Schedule III, 280E would no longer bar those deductions.

Research access

Schedule I comes with the tightest research controls. Under the April 2026 order, researchers who get marijuana products from a state licensee for scientific research won't face federal liability solely because of that source. Two conditions apply: the researcher must hold a DEA registration for marijuana research, and the licensee must have held a valid federal registration at the time of the transfer. The DEA also may not use a researcher's reliance on state-licensed products as grounds for action against the researcher's registration.

The December 2025 executive order that pushed the process forward was titled "Increasing Medical Marijuana and Cannabidiol Research." For the broader proposal, the 2024 notice added that research on a Schedule III substance may follow different DEA protocols than Schedule I research.

What rescheduling doesn't change

Rescheduling is a federal change, and a lot stays exactly where it was:

  • State law. The April 2026 order says it doesn't have substantial direct effects on the states. Michigan's adult-use and medical programs keep running under Michigan law.
  • Michigan's age and purchase rules. Adult-use buyers must be 21 or older, and stores check a valid ID before every sale. A single adult-use transaction is capped at 2.5 ounces, with no more than 15 grams as concentrate.
  • Crossing state lines. Taking cannabis across a state line remains illegal under federal law, even between two states where it's legal. The April order doesn't address interstate travel, and it doesn't say that patients may carry medical marijuana across state lines or onto federal property. Our guide to flying with cannabis covers air travel.
  • Federal jobs and firearms. The April order doesn't mention federal employment or gun purchases, and adult-use cannabis is still Schedule I. If either question affects you, talk to a lawyer before assuming anything has changed.
  • Legalization. Rescheduling isn't legalization. Even the broader proposal would keep marijuana under the federal law's criminal provisions.

At the counter in Michigan: what changes for shoppers

What rescheduling means for consumers depends on how you shop. For adult-use shoppers, nothing changes at the counter. You'll still show valid ID, the same purchase limits apply and Michigan's state taxes on adult-use sales stay in place.

For registered medical patients, the April order does cover marijuana sold under a state medical license. It's aimed at the businesses, though: their federal registration and how they dispense. It doesn't settle questions about travel or federal property.

A few practical reminders hold either way. Keep cannabis at home or another private place, since rescheduling doesn't change where you can use it. Don't drive after using it. And don't pack it for a trip out of state, whatever the schedule says.

Our Michigan cannabis laws guide covers possession, purchase limits and where you can use cannabis, and our FAQ answers common visit questions. At High Society, recreational shopping is for adults 21 and older with a valid government-issued ID, and that hasn't changed.

Next steps to watch

A few milestones will shape what happens to the broader proposal:

  1. The judge's recommended decision. This is the next formal step after the summer 2026 hearing.
  2. Exceptions from the parties. Designated participants may file objections for the DEA Administrator to consider.
  3. The DEA Administrator's final determination. This is the step that would decide whether all marijuana, including adult-use, moves into Schedule III.
  4. Effective dates and details. If a broader change is finalized, watch for when it takes effect and how it's carried out.

Timelines have slipped before, so be wary of predicted dates. To follow along, search the Federal Register for "rescheduling of marijuana," where the DEA publishes its notices.

Frequently asked questions

Did cannabis get rescheduled?

Partly. Since April 28, 2026, marijuana drugs approved by the FDA and marijuana covered by a state medical marijuana license have been in Schedule III. All other marijuana, including adult-use, remains Schedule I as of October 2026. A broader proposal to move all marijuana to Schedule III was still awaiting the judge's recommended decision in late October 2026.

What is the difference between Schedule I and Schedule III?

Schedule I is for drugs the federal government classifies as having high abuse potential and no currently accepted medical use. Schedule III covers drugs with an accepted medical use, lower abuse potential than Schedules I and II, and moderate or low physical dependence. Schedule III drugs are still controlled, and rescheduling alone doesn't make cannabis legal to sell or buy under federal law.

Will rescheduling make cannabis cheaper?

No one can say yet. In Schedule III, a business is no longer barred by Section 280E from deducting ordinary expenses on federal taxes, and the April 2026 order says this already applies to state medical licensees. Whether savings ever reach shelf prices depends on the market. Michigan's own taxes on adult-use sales are set by state law, which federal rescheduling doesn't change.

Can I take cannabis across state lines now?

No. Taking cannabis across a state line remains illegal under federal law, even between two states where it's legal, and Michigan law doesn't protect it. The April 2026 order doesn't address interstate travel, and it doesn't say patients may carry medical marijuana across state lines. Buy and enjoy cannabis in Michigan, and leave it at home when you travel.

Does rescheduling change Michigan law?

No. Michigan's adult-use and medical programs continue under state law, and the April 2026 order says it has no substantial direct effects on the states. You still need to be 21 or older with valid ID for adult-use purchases, stores check ID before every sale, and the same purchase limits apply.

  1. DOJ/DEA final rule: Rescheduling of FDA-Approved Products Containing Marijuana From Schedule I to Schedule III (91 FR 22714, April 28, 2026, effective April 28, 2026)federalregister.gov
  2. DEA: Rescheduling of Marijuana; withdrawal of the 2024 notice of hearing (FR Doc. 2026-08178, April 28, 2026)federalregister.gov
  3. DOJ notice of proposed rulemaking: Schedules of Controlled Substances: Rescheduling of Marijuana (89 FR 44597, May 21, 2024)federalregister.gov
  4. Morgan Lewis: High Time for a Change? Post-DEA Hearing, Broader Marijuana Rescheduling Questions Remain (September 24, 2026)morganlewis.com
  5. NORML (advocacy group) news report quoting the judge's order: DEA judge overseeing marijuana rescheduling permits parties to file additional briefs, denies request to reopen hearing (October 22, 2026)norml.org
  6. Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Marihuana Rules, R 420.1 to R 420.1004 (ID check before each sale, per-transaction limits)michigan.gov
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
